scenes.caption: What if the gods knew exactly how the world would end—and chose to face it anyway? The Norse called that ending Ragnarök.
It began with three terrible winters, one after another. No summer came. Families turned against each other, and the world grew cold.
Then a wolf swallowed the sun. Another seized the moon. The stars vanished, and the roots of Yggdrasil, the world tree, began to shake.
Fenrir, the giant wolf, shattered his chains. From the ocean rose Jörmungandr, the serpent that encircled the earth, dragging waves across the land.
Heimdall blew his horn. The gods armed themselves, and Odin rode at their head. The prophecy had told them how this battle would end.
Odin confronted Fenrir. The wolf swallowed the king of the gods. But Odin’s son, Víðarr, stepped forward and tore the beast apart.
Thor met the world serpent amid poisonous waves. His hammer killed Jörmungandr. Thor staggered nine steps away—then fell to the serpent’s venom.
And then Surtr came, his sword blazing brighter than the sun. Fire swept across the battlefield, and the old world sank beneath the sea.
For a moment, nothing remained. Then the water receded. Green earth rose again. The surviving gods returned, and two humans emerged to begin anew.
So Ragnarök was never only a prophecy of destruction. It was a story of courage in the face of fate—and of life after the end.
